title: Acute Confusion and Delirium
summary: A clinician-facing guide for recognising delirium, distinguishing it from baseline cognitive impairment, identifying reversible causes and arranging safe treatment and disposition.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: An acute or fluctuating change from the person’s usual cognition, attention, behaviour, alertness or function.
Hypoactive delirium, including unusual quietness, slow responses, reduced movement, withdrawal or reduced appetite.
Immediate physiological threats, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, sepsis, stroke, seizure, head injury or toxic-metabolic disturbance.
Pain, dehydration, constipation, urinary retention, medication toxicity, withdrawal and environmental triggers.
Baseline dementia or cognitive impairment without assuming this explains the acute change.
Capacity for the current decision and whether safe care can be delivered in the current environment.
items.importantLimitation: Delirium is a medical syndrome caused by one or more underlying problems. A normal temperature or NEWS2 does not exclude it.

items.title: Timeline and baseline
mustConfirmOrExclude: Last known normal cognition and function.
Onset over hours or days, fluctuation during the day and any lucid intervals.
Usual memory, communication, sleep, behaviour and independence.
Collateral history from family, carers or staff who know the person.

items.title: Associated symptoms and causes
mustConfirmOrExclude: Fever, respiratory, urinary, abdominal, skin or neurological symptoms.
Pain, fall, head injury, immobility or recent procedure.
Reduced intake, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation or urinary retention.
Recent medicine changes, missed doses, opioids, sedatives, anticholinergics, steroids or alcohol withdrawal.
Visual or hearing impairment, sleep disruption and unfamiliar surroundings.

items.title: Decision-making and immediate safety
mustConfirmOrExclude: Understanding, retention, use and weighing of information, and communication of the relevant decision.
Risk of wandering, falls, self-neglect, missed medicines, inability to eat or drink, and carer breakdown.
Advance care plans, treatment-escalation plans and preferred place of care.

items.title: Critical physiological or neurological abnormality
mustConfirmOrExclude: Airway, breathing or circulatory compromise; hypoxia; hypoglycaemia; severe temperature abnormality; or persistent haemodynamic instability.
New focal neurological deficit, seizure, meningism, severe headache, reduced consciousness or recent head injury.
Agitation, aggression, wandering or reduced arousal creating immediate risk that cannot be managed safely.

items.title: Serious reversible cause
mustConfirmOrExclude: Sepsis or significant infection, acute kidney injury, electrolyte disturbance, urinary retention, faecal impaction or uncontrolled pain.
Medicine toxicity, withdrawal, overdose, missed essential treatment or substance-related cause.
No safe supervision, inability to meet essential needs or concern for neglect or safeguarding.

items.title: Physiological and neurological screen
howToTest: Record full observations, glucose and level of consciousness.
Assess hydration, perfusion, respiratory status, pain and infection sources.
Perform a focused neurological examination and assess for injury.
normal: Physiology stable with no focal deficit or acute illness features.
abnormal: Hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, abnormal physiology, focal deficit, meningism, injury or altered consciousness.
implications: Treat time-critical causes immediately and escalate according to the suspected diagnosis.

items.title: 4AT delirium screen
howToTest: Assess alertness, the four-item Abbreviated Mental Test, attention using months backwards, and evidence of acute change or fluctuation.
Use collateral history to establish acute change.
normal: 4AT score 0 makes delirium less likely when no other concerning features are present.
abnormal: 4AT score 4 or more suggests possible delirium with or without cognitive impairment; scores 1 to 3 suggest possible cognitive impairment.
implications: The 4AT supports recognition but does not replace clinical assessment or investigation of the cause.

items.title: Infection
commonFindings: Respiratory, urinary, skin or abdominal symptoms may be subtle or absent.
implications: Investigate according to clinical findings; avoid diagnosing UTI from confusion alone without urinary or systemic evidence.

items.title: Metabolic or physiological disturbance
commonFindings: Hypoxia, glucose disturbance, dehydration, acute kidney injury, electrolyte abnormality or organ failure.
implications: Correct the disturbance and identify why it occurred.

items.title: Medication or substance-related
commonFindings: Recent initiation, dose increase, accumulation in renal impairment, anticholinergic burden, opioid or sedative effect, or withdrawal.
implications: Reconcile medicines and obtain prescriber or toxicology advice where needed.

items.title: Pain, urinary retention or constipation
commonFindings: Agitation or withdrawal without clear verbal complaint, suprapubic fullness, reduced bowel output or discomfort.
implications: Examine and treat the underlying problem while avoiding unnecessary sedating medication.

items.title: Delirium superimposed on dementia
commonFindings: Known chronic cognitive impairment with a new acute or fluctuating change.
implications: Treat as delirium and use collateral history to define baseline.

items.title: Initial management
mustConfirmOrExclude: Treat the identified cause or causes.
Provide orientation, familiar communication, hearing aids, glasses, hydration, pain relief and sleep support.
Minimise unnecessary moves, noise, restraint, catheters and sedating or anticholinergic medicines.
Involve family or carers where appropriate.

items.title: Hospital or urgent same-day assessment
mustConfirmOrExclude: Unclear cause, abnormal physiology, focal deficit, reduced consciousness, significant injury, inability to maintain intake or essential care, severe behavioural risk, carer breakdown or no reliable follow-up.

items.title: Home or community management
mustConfirmOrExclude: A clear treatable cause with an accepted pathway and named clinical follow-up.
Physiology stable and no time-critical diagnosis requiring hospital care.
Reliable supervision, food, fluids, medicines, toileting and urgent access to help.
Capacity or lawful best-interest decision-making documented.
A specific review time and escalation route.

items.title: Record explicitly
mustConfirmOrExclude: Exact acute change, onset, fluctuation and collateral source.
Baseline cognition and function.
4AT components and score, not only “confused”.
Potential causes considered and findings supporting or opposing each.
Capacity assessment for the relevant decision.
Treatment, supervision, review ownership and safety-netting.

items.title: Acute confusion and delirium
safetyNetting: Any significant deterioration in breathing, chest pain or collapse – call 999.

Seek urgent reassessment for increasing drowsiness, inability to wake normally, new weakness or speech change, seizure, inability to drink or pass urine, repeated vomiting, fever with deterioration, a fall or inability to provide safe supervision.

clinicalValidation.reviewNotes: Clinical validation required before publication. Core sources: NICE CG103, NICE NG5 and NICE NG56.
